title: Carried down by angel ambassadors.
subtitle: The messengers who bring the revelation
then: Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and others said the Safarah {idea}are the angels.{/idea} Al-Bukhari explained that they descend with Allah's revelation {reward}like the ambassador who rectifies matters between people.{/reward}
now: You pass on a forwarded message without checking it. A rumour travels through your office in a day. {idea}The Quran came through carriers who never twisted a word.{/idea} It asks you to be a careful carrier too.
old: How a message reaches me does not really matter.
new: The Quran reached me through honored hands, and I can pass it on with the same care.
try: Before forwarding anything today, check it first, or do not send it.

title: Noble carriers, and you can stand with them.
subtitle: The reciter's company with the angels
then: Ibn Kathir says the angels are {reward}noble and honorable{/reward}, righteous and pure in deeds. He cites the hadith from Aishah: the one who recites the Quran well {idea}will be with the noble, righteous ambassador angels{/idea}, and the one who struggles with it gets two rewards.
now: You stumble over the Arabic at night, sounding out each letter, and feel embarrassed. {reward}That stumbling earns double.{/reward} The fluent reciter at the masjid and you are both in good company.
old: My recitation is too poor to count for much.
new: Struggling through the Quran carries its own double reward.
try: Recite one short surah aloud today, slowly, even if you stumble.

title: How ungrateful man can be.
subtitle: Denial without any real argument
then: Ibn Abbas explained the opening word as a curse on man. Abu Malik said it refers to {trap}the rejecting type, who denies without any supporting argument{/trap}, simply because the Resurrection seems farfetched to him. The verses that follow answer that doubt.
now: You wake up breathing, eat breakfast you did not grow, and drive to work on a body you did not design. {trap}Gratitude can go missing in a normal morning.{/trap} The verse is a hard knock on that forgetfulness.
old: I am not ungrateful, I just do not think about it much.
new: Not thinking about where everything came from is its own kind of ingratitude.
try: Name three things you did not make but used before noon today, and thank Allah for each.

title: Ask yourself what you were made from.
subtitle: A question that shrinks arrogance
then: Ibn Kathir says Allah explains here {idea}how He created him from something despised{/idea}, and that {reward}He is able to bring him back to life just as He created him initially.{/reward} The question is meant to stop the denier in his tracks.
now: You scroll past a baby scan photo in the family group chat. A few weeks ago that child was almost nothing. {idea}So were you.{/idea} Pride gets quieter when you remember the start.
old: I have always been more or less who I am now.
new: I began as almost nothing, and the One who made me can make me again.
try: Look at a baby photo of yourself today and say a quiet alhamdulillah.

title: From a drop, with everything measured out.
subtitle: Your life was planned from its first moment
then: Ibn Kathir explains that Allah created man from a drop and then set him in proportion, meaning {idea}He decreed his life span, his sustenance, his deeds{/idea}, and whether he would be miserable or happy.
now: You lie awake doing salary maths, worried the provision will run out. {reward}Your provision was measured before you were born.{/reward} Your job is the effort. The amount is already written.
old: Everything in my life depends on my own planning.
new: My span and provision were set by Allah. My part is how I use them.
try: Tonight, before sleeping, hand one money worry to Allah in a short dua and leave it there.

title: Then He made the way easy for you.
subtitle: Birth, and the path laid clear
then: Ibn Abbas said it means {reward}He made his coming out of his mother's belly easy for him.{/reward} Mujahid linked it to 76:3, that Allah guided man on the path, grateful or ungrateful. Ibn Kathir calls this second view {idea}the most correct, and Allah knows best.{/idea}
now: You know where the prayer times are on your phone. You know which friend drags you down. {idea}Most of the path is already clear.{/idea} What is left is whether you walk it.
old: I would do better if the right way were clearer.
new: Allah has already made the way plain. The choice to walk it is mine.
try: Pick one good thing you already know you should do, and do it once today.

title: Then death, and a place in the earth.
subtitle: The grave is part of the honor
then: Ibn Kathir explains: {idea}after creating man, Allah causes him to die and makes him the inhabitant of a grave.{/idea} Creation, the easy path, then death. The sequence keeps moving because {reward}the story is not finished.{/reward}
now: You stand at a funeral in the rain, watching the earth go back over someone you knew. You check your phone in the car afterwards. {idea}That grave is a waypoint, not a full stop.{/idea}
old: Death is the end of the story and best not thought about.
new: Death and the grave are a stage Allah arranged, with more to come.
try: Visit a grave, or simply make dua today for one person you have lost.

title: When He wills, He raises you again.
subtitle: Resurrection as the next step
then: Ibn Kathir says this is called {idea}al-Ba'th and an-Nushur{/idea}, the resurrection. He cites 30:20 and 2:259, and the hadith in the Two Sahihs that every human decays except the tailbone, {reward}from which he will be reconstructed.{/reward}
now: You plant a seed in a pot on the windowsill and forget it. A week later there is green. {idea}Something that looked gone came back.{/idea} The verse asks you to take that seriously about yourself.
old: Being brought back after death is hard to believe.
new: The One who made me from nothing will raise me when He wills.
try: Say this once today with meaning: I will be raised, so let me live like it.

title: No, he has not done what he was told.
subtitle: The gap between claim and duty

row.title: Ibn Jarir
sub: man has not fulfilled his duty

row.title: Ibn Kathir
sub: the raising has not come yet

then: Ibn Jarir said the disbeliever {trap}claims he has fulfilled Allah's right upon him{/trap}, but he has not. Ibn Kathir adds another view: Allah has not yet resurrected them, {idea}until the time of humanity's earthly life is complete.{/idea}
now: You tick off your prayers and charity like a checklist and feel you are basically square with Allah. {trap}The feeling of being done is the danger.{/trap} There is still time left on the clock.
old: I have done enough. Allah and I are even.
new: I have not yet done all I was asked, and there is still time to do more.
try: Pick one duty you have been doing half-way, and do it fully once today.

title: Look at your plate.
subtitle: Food as a sign and a favor
then: Ibn Kathir says this is {reward}a call to reflect upon Allah's favor.{/reward} It is also evidence: {idea}vegetation coming to life from lifeless earth{/idea} shows bodies can be brought back after becoming dust.
now: You eat lunch at your desk while answering messages and could not say afterwards what it was. {idea}The verse says: stop and look at it.{/idea} Rice, bread, an apple. Each one came up out of dead ground.
old: Food is just fuel I grab between tasks.
new: Every meal is a gift and a quiet proof that life returns.
try: At your next meal, look at your food for ten seconds before eating, and say bismillah slowly.

title: It starts with water poured from the sky.
subtitle: The first step behind every meal
then: Ibn Kathir explains it plainly: {idea}We sent it down from the sky to the earth.{/idea} After calling man to look at his food, the verse goes back to the start of the chain. {reward}Every meal begins with rain.{/reward}
now: You leave the tap running while brushing your teeth. You complain when it rains on your commute. {reward}That same rain is in your breakfast.{/reward}
new: Rain is Allah pouring out the first step of my provision.
try: The next time it rains, say a short thank you instead of a complaint.

title: Then the ground splits open.
subtitle: Hard earth giving way to life
then: Ibn Kathir describes it: the water enters the earth and {idea}mingles with the parts of the seeds that are left in it.{/idea} From this {reward}the seeds grow, rise up and appear on the surface.{/reward}
now: You walk past a crack in the pavement and a green shoot is pushing through. {idea}Something soft beat something hard.{/idea} Your heart can feel like that pavement some weeks. It can still open.
old: Some things are too hard and closed to ever change.
new: Allah splits open what looks sealed, even the earth.
try: Look for one green thing growing in an unlikely place today and pause on it.

title: Grain, the quiet base of every table.
subtitle: Seeds that feed the world
then: Ibn Kathir says {reward}al-Habb refers to all types of seeds or grains.{/reward} The verse says Allah caused them to grow. The farmer plants, but {idea}the growing belongs to Him.{/idea}
now: Bread at breakfast, rice at dinner, pasta for the kids. {reward}Grain is in almost every meal you eat.{/reward} You have never once made a seed sprout by yourself.
new: Every grain I eat was grown by Allah from the dead ground.
try: Do not waste any bread or rice today. Finish it or save it.

title: Grapes for you, green fodder for the animals.
subtitle: Provision for people and livestock alike
then: Ibn Kathir says grapes are well known, and {reward}al-Qadb are the moist green plants that animals graze on.{/reward} Al-Hasan al-Basri said it is fodder. {idea}The same rain feeds your fruit and the animals' grass.{/idea}
now: You buy grapes at the market. The milk in your fridge came from a cow that ate grass. {idea}Both were on Allah's list.{/idea} Your food chain is longer than you think.
old: My food has nothing to do with animals in a field.
new: Allah feeds me and the animals that feed me, from the same earth.
try: Feed a bird or animal today, or put out water for one.
